title: GPT-3: How a 175-billion-parameter model learns new tasks with no fine-tuning, just a few examples
summary: GPT-3 scales the model to 175 billion parameters, then stops fine-tuning for each task: it only writes instructions and a few examples into the prompt. We unpack in-context learning, zero-shot to few-shot, the training data and the compute formula—where it shines, where it still falls short, and how the paper takes seriously the question of whether the test questions had been memorized.
ai_summary: GPT-3 (OpenAI, 2020) is a 175-billion-parameter autoregressive language model that uses the GPT-2 architecture and was trained on about 300 billion tokens. The paper's core idea is in-context learning: no parameters are updated; the prompt contains task instructions and 0, 1, or 10–100 examples. In the few-shot setting, GPT-3 reaches 71.2% on TriviaQA closed-book QA, 86.4% on LAMBADA, and beats fine-tuned BERT-LARGE on SuperGLUE; humans can distinguish its short news articles from human text only about 52% of the time. Weaknesses include comparison tasks such as WiC and ANLI, common-sense physics, and long-form coherence. The paper also systematically checks whether test questions leaked into training data, and discusses bias and energy use.
brief: Problem: Pre-training plus fine-tuning still demands thousands to tens of thousands of labeled examples for every task, while humans can pick up a new task from one or two examples.
Method: Scale the model to 175 billion parameters, specify the task through instructions and examples in the prompt, and change no parameters at all (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot).
Results: The larger the model, the better it uses examples; on closed-book QA and LAMBADA it matches or beats fine-tuned models, and it is also strong translating into English.
Limitations: Tasks that compare two pieces of text are near random; long-form output drifts; training costs about 3.14 × 10²³ floating-point operations; and the model inherits biases from its data.

paper.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
paper.authors: Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder, Melanie Subbiah, Jared Kaplan, Prafulla Dhariwal et al. (31 authors)

cover.headline: GPT-3: A close read of the original paper
cover.highlight: No fine-tuning, just a few examples

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In May 2020, 31 OpenAI authors released a 75-page paper introducing **GPT-3**: a 175-billion-parameter language model, 10× larger than any previous non-sparse language model. The architecture itself isn't new—it is essentially a scaled-up GPT-2. What is new is how they **use** it: they don't retrain or change a single parameter for any task. They describe the task in natural language in the input, optionally add a few examples, and the model does it.

This way of using the model already holds its own against models fine-tuned for the job. For trivia questions without any external sources (TriviaQA), few-shot accuracy is 71.2%, beating the best fine-tuned model under the same closed-book setting. Its roughly 200-word news articles are distinguished from human writing by ordinary readers only about 52% of the time—coin-flip territory. The paper also candidly lists its weak spots: tasks that judge the relationship between two sentences, some reading comprehension, and questions requiring common-sense physics remain poor.

The previous BERT close read showed that "pre-training + fine-tuning" works; GPT-3 takes the next step: **fine-tuning can be dropped altogether**. Today, when we write prompts with instructions and examples for ChatGPT or Claude, the systematic evidence for this way of using models comes from this paper.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: GPT-3 = a GPT-2 architecture scaled to 175 billion parameters + training on 300 billion tokens + a new way of using it: change no parameters at all, just write instructions in the input and give 0, 1, or dozens of examples (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot), and the model "learns" the task on the spot. The paper calls this **in-context learning**.

callout.title: Four useful concepts for this paper
callout.text: Don't worry if you're fuzzy on them; these four are enough:
list: **Autoregressive language model**: a model that predicts the next token from left to right, one token at a time—the decoder branch of the Transformer that "only looks left" (see our Transformer and BERT close reads).
**Token**: the basic unit the model reads and writes, a bit smaller than a word. The paper says its encoding averages about 0.7 English words per token.
**Parameters**: all the trainable numbers in the model. More parameters means the model can remember and represent more, but training and inference also cost more.
**Fine-tuning**: training the pre-trained model again on labeled data for a specific task, changing its parameters. This is the approach BERT uses.

sections.h: Before GPT-3: a labeled dataset for every task

blocks.p: After BERT, "pre-training + fine-tuning" became the standard recipe: you no longer need a task-specific architecture, but every task still requires **thousands to tens of thousands** of labeled examples for fine-tuning. The paper gives three reasons this should change:

list: **Practicality**: useful language tasks are endless—from fixing grammar to critiquing a short story—and most have no large existing labeled dataset; collecting one for every task is impossible.

**High scores can be misleading**: the larger the model and the narrower the fine-tuning data, the easier it is to pick up accidental shortcuts in the training data. The research the paper cites shows that "human-level" benchmark scores after fine-tuning may overstate the model's real ability on the underlying task.

**That's not how people learn**: a one-sentence instruction ("Tell me whether this sentence is happy or sad") or an example or two is enough for a person to start a new task, and to switch tasks in a long conversation.

blocks.p: GPT-2 had already tried having models learn tasks directly from prompts, but the results were far below fine-tuning: only 4% on open-domain question answering on Natural Questions, and its 55 F1 on CoQA reading comprehension was already more than 35 points behind the best result.

But another trend gave the authors confidence: Transformer language models had grown by two orders of magnitude in a few years, and every increase brought progress; another study (Scaling Laws, also on our reading list) found that loss declines **smoothly** with scale. Since in-context learning requires packing many skills into parameters, it should also improve with scale. So they pushed the model straight to 175 billion parameters.

fig.title: Language models grew more than 1,000× in a few years, and GPT-3 is 10× the previous largest
fig.subtitle: Unit: 100M parameters. The first six are models listed in the paper's introduction; amber is GPT-3.
fig.note: The paper gives this growth line as 100M, 300M, 1.5B, 8B, 11B, and 17B parameters. Model names and years were added by us using the paper's references.

sections.h: The core idea: in-context learning, plus zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot

blocks.p: The paper sees the whole process as two nested loops of "meta-learning": the outer loop is pre-training, where the model sees countless implicit small tasks in a huge text corpus and builds a broad set of skills and pattern-recognition abilities; the inner loop happens **within a single forward pass**: it reads the instructions and examples in the prompt, recognizes what to do, and continues writing. The paper calls the inner loop **in-context learning**.

callout.title: Like a well-read new colleague
callout.text: You hand a new colleague a spreadsheet and say, "Fill in the rest following the format of the first three rows." He hasn't been trained for this specific job, but because he has seen enough spreadsheets and work, a few example rows tell him what to do. GPT-3's "learning" is the same: it isn't a training session; it's understanding the examples you gave.

blocks.p: The paper divides the settings by how many examples are in the prompt, and contrasts them with traditional fine-tuning:

fig.title: Four settings: only fine-tuning changes parameters
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: examples we devised following the idea of the paper's Figure 2.1. The text after → is what the model is expected to write; amber is the paper's featured few-shot setting.
rows: A task; previously trained on a large labeled dataset
(First trained on thousands of translation examples) cheese → ?
Translate English into French: apple → pomme; cheese → ?
Translate English into French: apple → pomme; bicycle → vélo; …; cheese → ?

plain.title: Zero, one, or several examples
plain.text: Zero-shot tells the model only what to do; one-shot adds a single completed example; few-shot adds several examples. In all three, you just write a few more lines into the input—no parameters change. That is in-context learning.

blocks.p: How many examples fit in few-shot depends on how much the model can read at once: GPT-3's context window is 2,048 tokens, which typically holds 10 to 100 examples. The paper also calls out one-shot separately because it is closest to how people assign tasks: on a crowdsourcing platform, you usually include one demonstration.

callout.title: In few-shot mode, the model is not "learning" any parameters
callout.text: The "learning" in few-shot does not change any parameter in the model. Examples are just read as part of the input; once this answer ends, the next prompt has no memory of those examples. The paper stresses that the "learning curves" that rise with more examples involve no gradient updates—only more conditioning.

blocks.p: There's also a question the paper itself can't settle: at inference time, is the model **learning** a new task from scratch, or just **recognizing** a task it saw during pre-training? The paper thinks different tasks may fall at different points on a spectrum: artificial tasks like unscrambling words look more like learning on the spot, while translation is clearly something pre-training already taught. This is revisited in the limitations section.

quiz.q: After GPT-3 completes 1,000 translation questions in the few-shot setting, what happens to its parameters?
options: It is fine-tuned on those 1,000 questions
No change at all
Only the last layer is updated
It updates after every question
quiz.why: Few-shot, one-shot, and zero-shot all do only a "forward pass" with no gradient updates. Examples are written into the input as conditioning, then discarded. The only way to change parameters is fine-tuning, and the paper explicitly says GPT-3 was not fine-tuned.

sections.h: How scoring works: probabilities for multiple choice, direct generation for free-form tasks

blocks.p: A model with no fine-tuning has no task-specific "classification head", so how does it answer multiple-choice questions? The paper's method: append each candidate answer to the question and see which one the model thinks is **most likely** to come next.

But comparing the probability of whole answers has a trap: longer answers multiply more probabilities, so their total probability is naturally smaller. The paper therefore compares the **average per-token log-likelihood** on most tasks:

formula.expr: score(answer) = (1 / L) · Σᵢ log P(tokenᵢ | question, previous answer tokens)

parts.desc: The number of tokens in this candidate answer
The log-probability the model assigns to token i appearing here; the closer to 0, the more confident
Sum the log-probabilities of all tokens and divide by length—that is, take the average—to remove the effect of length

formula.note: On ARC, OpenBookQA, and RACE, the paper further divides by the probability of the answer following a common prefix ("Answer: ") to counteract the effect of some answers being more common in general.

plain.title: Compare the average per-token score
plain.text: Longer answers multiply more probabilities, so their total probability is smaller—long answers are naturally at a disadvantage. Correct answer A flows smoothly at each step (0.8) but is longer; wrong answer B is short, but each step is shakier. Compare average log-probability per token: A's -0.22 beats B's -0.43, so the model picks correctly.

fig.title: Total probability would pick the wrong answer; averaging by length picks the right one
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: probabilities are invented, not from the paper. Question: "At what temperature does water boil under standard atmospheric pressure?" Amber is the correct answer.
fig.note: The correct answer is smooth at every step (0.8) but longer; the wrong answer is shorter but shakier at every step. Total probability: 0.420 beats 0.328, so it would pick wrong. Average log-probability: -0.22 beats -0.43, so it picks right.

blocks.p: For open-ended tasks such as translation or QA, the model generates directly with beam search (beam width 4, length penalty α = 0.6, as in the original Transformer paper), then scores with F1, BLEU, or exact match as usual for each dataset. Few-shot examples are sampled randomly from the task's training set, separated by one or two newlines.

quiz.q: Why compare "average per-token likelihood" rather than total probability for multiple-choice?
options: Because the model can only compute averages
Because longer answers multiply more probabilities below 1, so their total probability is naturally smaller and unfair
Because short answers are usually wrong
Because it is faster to compute
quiz.why: Every token's probability is below 1, so multiplying more produces a smaller number. If you compare total probability directly, the model will systematically favor short answers. Averaging measures "how natural each step is," independent of answer length.

sections.h: The model: a scaled-up GPT-2, trained in eight sizes

blocks.p: GPT-3's architecture is essentially the same as GPT-2, including pre-normalization: layer normalization is moved before each sub-layer. The only change is alternating between dense attention and "locally banded" sparse attention in different layers, an idea from Sparse Transformer. The feed-forward width is always 4× the model dimension, and all models have a 2,048-token context window.
To study scale, they trained eight sizes at once, from 125 million to 175 billion parameters—three orders of magnitude—and **each one was trained on 300 billion tokens**.

fig.title: Five of eight sizes: larger models use bigger batches and smaller learning rates
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 2.1. Batch size is in tokens; amber is the full GPT-3.

blocks.p: An empirical pattern emerges: larger models can use larger batches but need smaller learning rates. The paper sets batch size from the measured "gradient noise scale" during training. All models were trained on V100 GPUs in a high-bandwidth cluster provided by Microsoft; to fit, the model was partitioned across GPUs both by layer and by matrix.

callout.title: A small exercise to check you really read the table
callout.text: Normally, "heads × per-head dimension" should equal the model dimension: Small is 12 × 64 = 768, and 175B is 96 × 128 = 12,288—both check out. But the XL row is 24 × 128 = 3,072, which doesn't match 2,048; the 13B row is 40 × 128 = 5,120, which is 20 away from 5,140. The paper doesn't explain these; they may be typos or implementation quirks. When reading papers, this habit of doing the multiplication yourself often reveals things the text won't tell you.

sections.h: Data: from 45TB down to 570GB, sampled by quality, not size

blocks.p: The main training corpus is Common Crawl, a public dataset that continuously crawls the web, with close to a trillion words—enough that the largest model sees each piece of text only once. But the authors found that lightly filtered Common Crawl was clearly lower quality than curated corpora, so they did three things:

list: **Filtering**: using a set of high-quality reference texts as a standard, keep only pages similar to them. They downloaded 41 monthly snapshots covering 2016–2019: 45TB of compressed text before filtering, 570GB after—about 400 billion tokens.
**Deduplication**: fuzzy document-level deduplication within and between datasets, and they ensured the held-out validation set doesn't overlap with training.
**Adding curated corpora**: an expanded WebText, two internet book collections (Books1, Books2), and English Wikipedia.

fig.title: Mix ratios are not proportional to size: Wikipedia is read 3.4 times, Common Crawl less than once
fig.subtitle: From the paper's Table 2.2; "passes" is how many times each dataset is passed over during the 300 billion training tokens. Amber is Wikipedia, the most read.

blocks.p: The authors deliberately sample higher-quality data more often, accepting slight overfitting on those sources in exchange for higher overall data quality. By word count, 93% of the training data is English and the remaining 7% is in other languages—something that will matter when the translation results are explained.

quiz.q: Wikipedia has only 3 billion tokens but is passed over 3.4 times during training; Common Crawl has 410 billion tokens but is passed over only 0.44 times. Why is that?
options: Wikipedia is updated more often.
The authors assign sampling ratios by quality rather than volume, and are willing to let high-quality data be seen more often.
Half of Common Crawl's data is corrupted.
It was a mistake in the training process.
quiz.why: The paper is explicit: sampling is not proportional to dataset size. It argues that higher-quality datasets are sampled more often, trading a little overfitting for higher data quality. Wikipedia makes up 3% of training, so its 3 billion tokens must supply 300 billion × 3% = 9 billion tokens of training—meaning it repeats about 3 times.

blocks.p: Appendix D of the paper offers a way to estimate training compute that is simple enough to do mentally. Ignoring the attention computation itself (the authors say it is usually less than 10% of the total), for each parameter on each token:

formula.expr: Total training compute C ≈ 6 · N · D

parts.desc: Model parameter count: GPT-3 175B actually has 174.6 billion.
In the forward pass, each parameter does one multiply and one add, counted as 2 floating-point operations; backpropagation is roughly twice the forward pass, adding another 4, for 6 total.

formula.note: Plugging in: 6 × 174.6 billion × 300 billion ≈ 3.14 × 10²³ floating-point operations, matching Table D.1 in the paper—about 3,640 petaflop/s-days (a petaflop/s-day is one quadrillion operations per second, sustained for a day).

plain.title: About 6 operations per parameter per token.
plain.text: In the forward pass, each parameter does roughly one multiply and one add per token; backpropagation is roughly twice the forward pass. Together that is about 6 operations per parameter per token. Multiply parameters by tokens by 6 and you get the total training computation.

fig.title: GPT-3's training compute is about 600× that of BERT-LARGE.
fig.subtitle: Units: petaflop/s-day, from Table D.1 of the paper. Amber is GPT-3 175B.
fig.note: "About 600×" was calculated by us from the table: 3640 ÷ 6.16 ≈ 591.

blocks.p: The paper also makes an interesting observation: according to the Scaling Laws analysis, the larger models were trained on far fewer tokens than usual. As a result, GPT-3 3B—as the paper writes it, though the table lists 2.7B—has nearly 10× the parameters of RoBERTa-LARGE yet uses about the same compute: roughly 50 petaflop/s-days.

Training is expensive, but using the trained model is not: the paper estimates that generating 100 pages of content with the trained 175-billion-parameter model uses about 0.4 kWh, costing only a few cents.

quiz.q: Use 6·N·D to estimate: GPT-3 13B actually has 12.85 billion parameters and is also trained on 300 billion tokens. About how many floating-point operations is its training compute?
options: About 2.3 × 10²⁰
About 2.3 × 10²²
About 2.3 × 10²⁴
About 3.9 × 10¹²
quiz.why: 6 × 12.85 billion × 300 billion = 6 × 1.285 × 10¹⁰ × 3 × 10¹¹ ≈ 2.31 × 10²², matching the 2.31E+22 for GPT-3 13B in Table D.1. Remember this formula: once you know any model's parameter count and training tokens, you can estimate how much compute it took.

sections.h: Results: bigger models, more examples, clearer gains.

blocks.p: The paper evaluates all eight models under the three settings on more than twenty datasets. Aggregating the 42 accuracy-scored benchmarks (the paper cautions that this aggregate is not itself a rigorous benchmark), zero-shot performance rises steadily with model size, while few-shot rises **faster**: the larger the model, the better it uses the examples in the prompt. Here are a few representative results:

fig.title: A few representative tasks: some already beat fine-tuned models, others still trail far behind.
fig.subtitle: From Tables 3.1–3.3 and 3.8 in the paper, GPT-3 175B. "Previous best" is mostly fine-tuned models; the blue columns are few-shot.
rows: LAMBADA (guess the last word of a passage, accuracy)

list: **LAMBADA**: you need the whole passage to guess its final word. Some had argued that further scaling would bring diminishing returns here, yet GPT-3 zero-shot already beats the previous best by 8 percentage points. Few-shot has a clever extra effect: the examples teach the model to "fill in just one word" rather than continue writing at length, lifting accuracy to 86.4%.

**Closed-book QA**: no external sources allowed—everything must come from knowledge stored in the parameters. On TriviaQA, zero-shot already beats all closed-book fine-tuned models (the best is 60.5); one-shot matches an open-book system that was both fine-tuned and able to retrieve 21 million documents; few-shot adds another 3.2 percentage points. The paper reads this as evidence that larger models store more knowledge in their parameters.

**SuperGLUE**: few-shot (32 examples per task) scores 71.8 overall, beating fine-tuned BERT-LARGE (69.0) but still far from the best result of 89.0. The paper finds that fewer than 8 examples per task are enough to beat fine-tuned BERT-LARGE on aggregate score.

**Obvious weaknesses**: on WiC, which asks whether a word means the same thing in two sentences, few-shot scores only 49.4%—coin-flip territory. On ANLI, an adversarial sentence-inference task, models smaller than GPT-3 are near random. The paper concludes that GPT-3 especially struggles with tasks that require comparing two pieces of text.

fig.title: Translation: strong into English, weak out of English.
fig.subtitle: Units: BLEU, from Table 3.4 of the paper. Blue columns are translation into English.
fig.note: When translating into English, few-shot GPT-3 beats prior unsupervised methods by about 5 BLEU, and on French and German it even surpasses the supervised best results shown in the table. Translating out of English is clearly weaker. The likely reason is that 93% of its training data is English: it is a strong "English writer."

sections.h: Custom-designed tasks: arithmetic, word scrambling, news writing

blocks.p: To check whether the model is just "memorizing" things seen in training, the authors designed a batch of tasks almost impossible to find verbatim on the web.

fig.title: Few-shot arithmetic: near-perfect on two-digit addition and subtraction, only about 10% on five-digit
fig.subtitle: Units: accuracy %, GPT-3 175B few-shot, 2,000 random problems per item. "1-digit mixed" means problems like 9×(7+5). From Table 3.9 of the paper; amber is two-digit addition.
fig.note: For three-digit addition, the main text says 80.2% while Table 3.9 says 80.4%—an inconsistency the paper does not explain.

blocks.p: Arithmetic performance has a clear "break": the second-largest model, 13B, gets only about half of two-digit addition and subtraction right and under 10% on the other operations; reliability appears suddenly at 175B. To rule out memorization, the authors searched the training data for three-digit problems: only 17 of 2,000 addition problems (0.8%) and 2 of 2,000 subtraction problems were found. The errors are also revealing: the model often **forgets to carry**, which suggests it is actually trying to compute rather than looking up answers.

fig.title: Word scrambling: almost zero zero-shot, learns from examples; reversed words never succeed
fig.subtitle: Units: accuracy %, GPT-3 175B, from Table 3.10 of the paper. Amber is reversed words.
rows: Shuffle middle letters (keep 2 at each end)
Shuffle middle letters (keep 1 at each end)

callout.title: Why reverse-spelling is so hard: the model doesn't see letters
callout.text: GPT-3 reads tokens, and on average one token is about 0.7 English words; common words are often a single token. For the model, "objects" may just be one whole unit. To spell it backwards, the model would first need to split that unit back into letters and recombine them, but it was never taught which letters make up each token. The paper notes that these tasks test not just handling tokens, but understanding the structure inside tokens.

blocks.p: **News writing**: the authors took 25 headlines and subheadings from news websites, had models of various sizes continue each into an article of about 200 words, and then asked about 80 US participants to judge whether each article was human-written or machine-written. To verify that participants were paying attention, they also included a deliberately bad "control model."

fig.title: The larger the model, the harder it is for people to tell: at 175B, only 2 points above chance
fig.subtitle: Units: share of human judgments that are correct, % (50% is chance). From Table 3.11 of the paper; amber is GPT-3 175B.
fig.note: The trend is generally downward, but not monotonic at every step (Large is easier to detect than Medium). With longer articles of about 500 words, human accuracy on GPT-3 remains only about 52%.

blocks.p: The paper also cautions that automatic detection tools may be better than humans at spotting machine-written text; factual errors, repetition, and incoherence are common giveaways. On SAT analogy questions, GPT-3 scores 65.2% few-shot, compared with 57% for the average college applicant that year (random guessing is 20%).

quiz.q: In the news experiment, human accuracy on GPT-3 175B articles is about 52%. How should we interpret that number?
options: 52% of people were fooled, and 48% were not.
Human judgment is about coin-flip level; people basically can't tell the difference.
GPT-3 wrote 52% of the articles better than humans.
It means half the news was written by GPT-3.
quiz.why: This measures the "share of correct judgments"; chance is 50%. 52% is only slightly above chance, meaning ordinary readers essentially can't tell the difference. The paper also notes that the larger the model, the more time participants spent per article—yet they became less and less able to distinguish human from machine.

sections.h: Data contamination: the test questions may already be in the training data

blocks.p: One of the most instructive parts of this paper is how seriously it treats a problem many people ignored at the time: training data is scraped from the whole web, and many benchmark questions are themselves on the web. If the model saw the test questions during training, high scores could simply be "memorized answers."

The authors originally planned to remove all test-set overlap before training, but a bug in the filtering pipeline removed only part of it—and retraining was too expensive. So they took a different approach: for each benchmark, they built a "clean subset" by removing any problem that shared 13 consecutive words with the training data (a deliberately strict criterion), then compared performance on the full set and the clean subset. If the two were similar, contamination—even if present—had not affected the results.

fig.title: Benchmarks checked individually: mostly false alarms, two marked with an asterisk
fig.subtitle: From Section 4 of the paper. The two amber rows are results marked with an asterisk in the main text.
rows: Only the source passages appeared, not the QA pairs themselves, so the model couldn't have memorized the answers
Only monolingual snippets about the same news events overlap, not paired translation data
Probably a statistical bias rather than memorization, but this cannot be strictly proven
Found 132 questions really in the training set, just in a different format
These results are simply not reported

blocks.p: The overall conclusion: although many benchmarks have high "possible contamination" rates (a quarter exceed 50%), in most cases the performance change is negligible, and there is no visible relationship between contamination rate and performance change. For language modeling, the paper mainly reports PTB precisely because it predates the modern internet and is uncontaminated.

callout.title: A question to ask of any future "record-breaking" large model
callout.text: The model trains on web-wide data—could the test questions be in there too? What checks did the paper run? Do the clean-subset results still hold? GPT-3's section gives a good template: acknowledge the problem, quantify the impact, and flag suspicious results.

quiz.q: If a model scores about the same on a benchmark's clean subset and its full set, what is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The benchmark is completely uncontaminated.
Even if contamination exists, it did not visibly inflate the scores.
The model memorized all the questions.
The benchmark is too easy.
quiz.why: The clean subset is what remains after removing all suspected leaked questions. Similar scores on both mean the suspected leaks didn't help the model, so contamination—if present—did not materially affect the results. It doesn't prove there was no contamination at all; the paper also says its detection method is conservative and may overstate contamination.

sections.h: Limitations: what the paper itself concedes

list: **Long-form text drifts**: generated text becomes semantically repetitive at the document level, loses coherence as it grows longer, contradicts itself, and occasionally produces non sequiturs.
**Common-sense physics**: questions like "If you put cheese in the fridge, will it melt?" are clearly hard for GPT-3.

**Comparison tasks**: deciding whether a word means the same thing in two sentences, or whether one sentence entails another, is barely above chance even few-shot. The paper suggests this may be because the model **can only read left-to-right**—the very value of bidirectionality that the BERT paper emphasized. It also speculates that a similarly large bidirectional model would perform better after fine-tuning.

**The limits of the pre-training objective**: the current objective treats every token equally and doesn't know which ones matter more; the model also hasn't seen video, the physical world, or other non-linguistic experience. The paper argues that simply scaling up "predict the next word" will eventually hit a ceiling, and suggests directions including **learning objectives from humans, fine-tuning with reinforcement learning**, and adding other modalities such as images.
**Data-hungry learning**: at inference it needs only a few examples, but during pre-training it reads far more text than a person sees in a lifetime.
**Expensive and unwieldy**: such a large model is costly at inference, and the paper proposes distilling it into smaller task-specific models.

**Bias**: the model inherits biases from its training data. For example, after phrases like "The {occupation} was a," across the 388 occupations tested, 83% were more likely to be followed by male terms; this was especially pronounced for higher-education occupations and heavy physical labor.

blocks.p: The suggestion to "learn objectives from humans and fine-tune with reinforcement learning" became InstructGPT two years later (2022): using human feedback to train GPT-3 to follow instructions—and after that came ChatGPT. That paper is also on our reading list.

callout.title: A few small blemishes in the paper
callout.text: If you read closely enough, you'll notice: three-digit addition is 80.2% in the main text and 80.4% in the table; the evaluation notes say "only the 200B few-shot result was submitted," but there is no 200B model—it should be 175B; and in Table 2.1, two rows have "heads × per-head dimension" that doesn't match the model dimension. None of this changes the conclusions, but it's a reminder that papers are written by people and numbers should be cross-checked.

sections.h: Check yourself: have you really absorbed it?

quiz.q: What is the difference among zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot?
options: The amount of training data differs.
The number of examples in the prompt at inference differs: 0, 1, or typically 10 to 100.
The model size differs.
The number of fine-tuning epochs differs.
quiz.why: All three use the same, completely unchanged model. The only difference is how many demonstrations are in the prompt: zero-shot has just the task instruction, one-shot adds one example, and few-shot uses as many as fit in the context window (typically 10 to 100).

quiz.q: The paper says GPT-3 does poorly on WiC, ANLI, and similar "compare two pieces of text" tasks. What is one possible structural reason?
options: The model has too few parameters.
It is an autoregressive model that can only read left-to-right, unlike bidirectional models that can see both sides at every position.
There is no English in the training data.
The context window is too long.
quiz.why: The paper states this hypothesis explicitly in the limitations section: they studied only autoregressive models, not bidirectional ones, which may hurt on tasks that require looking back to compare two passages or reading a long passage carefully before giving a short answer. This echoes the argument of the BERT paper.

callout.title: By the end, you should be able to answer these five questions in your own words.
list: What is “in-context learning”? What is its most fundamental difference from fine-tuning?
Why did the authors believe that making the model larger would also strengthen in-context learning?
When estimating a model's training compute with 6·N·D, what does each letter stand for?
Why is GPT-3 strong translating into English and weak translating out of English? Why can't it reverse-spell words?
What is data contamination? How does the paper check for it?
